old: (no explicit statement of how Pyramid_Level relates to Evidence_Tier)
new:
These categories describe the form a publication takes, not the strength of its evidence — which is why they sit outside the pyramid rather than inside it. They account for the remaining — studies, so the pyramid's — and these together add up to the full Atlas.

How this relates to the A–D tier. Pyramid level and evidence tier are two different axes. Every eligible peer-reviewed primary study receives an A–D tier. Narrative reviews are also peer-reviewed, so they carry the weakest tier (D) rather than no tier at all — but they sit outside the pyramid because a review is not itself an experiment. Preprints and registered trials receive no A–D tier in either direction: a preprint has not been reviewed, and a registered trial has no results yet, so grading them would invent a strength that does not exist. They are labelled as what they are.
why: Closes the last internal inconsistency: states plainly that narrative reviews get tier D while preprints and registered trials get no A-D tier, so 'every eligible peer-reviewed primary study is A-D graded' cannot be misread as 'everything is graded'.
